subject: Backward compatibility vs. forward compatibility (definitions)
description: This pairing is foundational orientation for the whole schema-evolution space: backward compatibility lets you upgrade consumers before producers (and rewind a consumer to the start of a topic and still read old data with the new schema); forward compatibility lets you upgrade producers before consumers. Without this distinction a reader cannot correctly reason about upgrade ordering at all, which is why it sits at orientation rather than operation.

subject: Definition of a breaking change (Microsoft REST API Guidelines)
description: This is orientation-level: without this definition a reader cannot correctly classify any specific change as breaking or safe, which blocks everything downstream (versioning, deprecation, governance). Concrete examples the guidelines list as breaking: removing or renaming APIs or parameters, behavioral changes to existing APIs, changes to error codes and fault contracts, and anything that violates the 'principle of least astonishment.' The guidelines flag that even additive changes like new JSON response fields can break naive clients that do strict schema validation, which is why they insist each service publish its own explicit definition rather than relying on a universal one.

subject: Pact: consumer-driven contract testing workflow
description: This is orientation-level because it establishes what consumer-driven contract testing fundamentally is and how it differs from schema-first approaches: rather than a static schema describing every possible interaction, the contract is generated from the consumer's actual usage, so 'only parts of the communication that are actually used by the consumer(s) get tested.' Pact's own docs describe the analogy of testing a smoke alarm's contract with its test button rather than by setting the house on fire - i.e. verifying integration without running both real services together end-to-end.

subject: REST versioning strategy: media-type (Content-Type) versioning
description: The Zalando compatibility chapter states the rule as a MUST: a major version number embedded in the path (e.g. /v1/customers) is disallowed because it creates 'tighter coupling and complexer release management' between provider and consumer release cycles. The mandated alternative is media-type versioning via HTTP content negotiation: the version travels in the Content-Type header as a parameter on a custom media type, e.g. application/x.<custom-media-type>+json;version=<version>. Zalando frames this as a last resort, though: the guidelines' stronger preference is to avoid versioning altogether by evolving the API through backward-compatible extensions, and to version only when a compatible extension is impossible.

subject: REST versioning strategy: query-string parameter
description: Guidelines.md section 12 presents query-string versioning (https://api.contoso.com/products/users?api-version=1.0) alongside URI-path versioning as the two primary schemes, plus an optional date-grouped variant (YYYY-MM-DD) that maps internally to Major.Minor. The guide is explicit about when each applies: 'Services guaranteeing URL path stability across versions may adopt query strings; services unable to ensure path stability must embed versions in the URI path.' This makes the choice conditional on an operational guarantee, not a stylistic preference.

subject: REST versioning strategy: URI path segment
description: Both the Microsoft REST API Guidelines and Google's AIP-185 describe URI-path versioning as a first-class option: the version appears as a leading path segment (Microsoft: /v1.0/products; Google: the major version is the first path component, e.g. /v1/). Microsoft's guideline requires that 'services co-located behind a DNS endpoint MUST use the same versioning mechanism' so that a single gateway can route consistently. Google AIP-185 additionally requires pre-stable versions to suffix the stability level onto the version segment (v1beta, v1alpha) while stable versions carry no suffix. The tradeoff versus header/media-type schemes: URI versioning is transparent and cache-friendly but couples the URL itself to the version, so migrating consumers means changing every call site. [AUDIT viable->wounded: 'the most common versioning scheme', 'cache-friendly' and 'routable by gateways' appear in NEITHER cited source. Microsoft's Guidelines.md presents path versioning as one of two options with the rule 'Services that cannot ensure URL path stability across future versions MUST embed the version in the URL path'; it never characterises it that way. The description also attributes the co-location MUST to gateway routing, whereas the document's stated reason is 'a consistent user experience across the endpoint is paramount.' Relabel the rationale as interpretation.]

subject: Avro aliases allow renaming fields without breaking readers
description: Without aliases, renaming a field would be indistinguishable to the resolution algorithm from removing one field and adding an unrelated one (since matching is by name) - which would silently lose data rather than fail loudly. Aliases are the specific mechanism that makes renaming a compatible, correctly-round-tripping change instead of a data-loss trap.

subject: Avro field defaults enable safe field addition and removal
description: This is the concrete mechanism behind 'you can add or remove Avro fields compatibly': addition is safe if the new field carries a default (so old data missing it resolves to the default), and removal is safe because the reader ignoring an unknown writer field never fails. Field order in the schema does not matter for resolution - the spec explicitly notes fields are matched by name, so reordering a schema's field list is itself a non-breaking, cosmetic change.

subject: Avro schema resolution: structural matching and type promotion
description: This is the mechanical rulebook a reader must follow to deserialize Avro data correctly whenever writer and reader schemas differ, which is the normal case in any evolving system - so it is operation-level, not orientation, because getting it wrong produces an immediate, visible deserialization failure or misread value. The specification is explicit that 'a reader must use the schema used by the writer' as an input to resolution, i.e. Avro readers need both schemas, unlike self-describing formats.

subject: Consistent versioning mechanism required across co-located services
description: Guidelines.md states this as a MUST-level rule under the versioning section. Mixing schemes behind one endpoint breaks routing assumptions immediately and visibly - a gateway configured to parse path-segment versions will silently mis-route (or fail to route) a request that instead carries its version in a query string, and vice versa. This is a correctness rule for using the chosen scheme, not a strategy choice itself. [AUDIT viable->wounded: The MUST-level rule is real and quoted correctly ('Services co-located behind a DNS endpoint MUST use the same versioning mechanism'), but the stated reason -- 'because a gateway or client library cannot correctly dispatch a mix' and 'a gateway configured to parse path-segment versions will silently mis-route' -- is not the document's rationale. Guidelines.md gives 'a consistent user experience across the endpoint is paramount.' Unsupported mechanism attached to a supported rule, labeled cited fact.]

subject: Deprecation and Sunset link relations for policy documentation
description: The header alone only carries a date; the link relation is how a provider attaches an explanation. Zalando's own deprecation guidance builds on the same pattern, requiring producers to add a description explaining the deprecation and provide a migration manual - the RFC-level link relation is the standard mechanism for surfacing exactly that kind of documentation to automated clients rather than only humans reading changelogs.

subject: Deprecation HTTP response header (RFC 9745)
description: The RFC pairs the header with a 'deprecation' link relation that servers can use to point clients at documentation about the deprecation policy or migration path. It explicitly integrates with the Sunset header from RFC 8594: per RFC 9745, the timestamp in Sunset must not precede the Deprecation date, since deprecation (advance notice) logically precedes sunset (actual retirement).

subject: Google AIP: APIs must not expose minor or patch version numbers
description: This is stricter than Microsoft's Major.Minor convention: Google's model treats every non-breaking change as an in-place update to the same major version, so minor/patch numbers would be meaningless noise to the consumer. The rule is specifically about what appears in the interface surface (package name, URI path), not about internal build or release tracking.

subject: Kafka Streams requires BACKWARD-only compatibility and upgrade-before-producer ordering
description: This is a specific operational constraint that breaks visibly and immediately if violated: if a producer starts writing a new (even backward-compatible) schema version before the downstream Streams app has been upgraded, the Streams app fails to process the new records correctly. It's called out separately from the general BACKWARD/FORWARD/FULL mode description because it's a constraint on a specific consumer technology (Kafka Streams), not a property of the compatibility mode itself. [MERGED FROM A-040] The underlying reason: a Streams application reads both new input topics and its own older internal state stores, so it must tolerate old data under a new schema.

subject: Major.Minor version numbering convention
description: Guidelines.md ties the numbering scheme directly to the breaking-change definition elsewhere in the same document: a breaking change requires a major-version bump, while backward-compatible additions may use a minor-version bump. This gives consumers a mechanical way to know, from the number alone, whether an upgrade requires code changes.

subject: Microsoft Graph's catalogue of breaking vs. non-breaking changes
description: Graph's own working definition: 'any change that requires a client to change its implementation to continue working with the service.' This catalogue operationalizes that definition into a checklist a reviewer can apply directly to a proposed change, which is what distinguishes it from the orientation-level definition alone - this is the concrete list you apply correctly in the normal case, and getting an item wrong (e.g. treating a non-nullable property addition as safe) breaks clients immediately upon deployment.

subject: Ordering constraint between Deprecation and Sunset header dates
description: This is a specific correctness rule for using the two headers together: violating it produces a logically incoherent signal to clients (retirement before notice of deprecation), which breaks the trust a client places in the headers to plan its migration. It sits at the operation level because getting it wrong is a visible, mechanical spec violation, not a strategic tradeoff.

subject: Per-subject vs. global compatibility configuration in Schema Registry
description: Knowing this override relationship is necessary to use the registry correctly day-to-day: an operator who only checks the global config can be surprised by a subject that was deliberately configured looser or stricter. This is a mechanical configuration fact, not a strategy choice, so it sits at operation.

subject: Protobuf field numbers are permanent wire identifiers
description: This is the single most load-bearing operation-level rule in Protobuf schema evolution: field names can be freely changed (they don't appear on the wire at all, only in generated source), but field numbers are the actual identity of a field to any decoder, old or new. Violating it doesn't produce a compile error - it silently corrupts data at runtime, which is exactly the kind of immediate-but-easy-to-miss failure that defines the operation tier.

subject: Protobuf reserved fields prevent number/name reuse after deletion
description: This directly operationalizes the field-number-permanence rule from the companion row: deleting a field without reserving its number leaves a trap for a future developer who might unknowingly reassign that number to an unrelated field, which would then be misinterpreted by any old client still emitting the deleted field's data under the old number. Reserving both the numeric tag and the textual name closes both halves of that gap.

subject: Schema Registry compatibility modes: BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL
description: BACKWARD is the Schema Registry default and Confluent's stated preferred mode for Kafka specifically because it lets you rewind consumers to the beginning of a topic and still deserialize with the new schema. FULL is the most restrictive but lets producers and consumers upgrade independently in any order, which matters when you cannot guarantee upgrade sequencing across teams. Getting the allowed-changes list wrong (e.g. adding a required field under BACKWARD) fails the registry's compatibility check immediately at schema-registration time - a visible, operation-level failure.

subject: Sunset HTTP response header (RFC 8594)
description: The RFC frames the sunset date as a hint, not a guarantee - clients should not treat it as a hard contractual deadline, only as a signal to plan migration. It is distinct from HTTP caching headers: Sunset communicates resource retirement, not content freshness. Documented use cases include temporary resources, service migrations, regulatory retention windows, and API deprecation specifically.

subject: Avro fields without default values
description: The Avro specification (opened directly) defines schema resolution precisely: if the reader's schema has a field with no matching field in the writer's schema and that reader field has no default value, 'an error is signalled' — not a null, not a skip. Default values are what let a reader schema fill in a value for a field the writer's schema didn't have. A second, less obvious point from the same spec: 'the presence of a default value does not make the field optional at encoding time. Avro encodes a field even if its value is equal to its default' — so a default solves the reader-compatibility problem but does not make the field optional for writers. The common mistake is adding a field to an Avro schema and assuming it's safe because Avro schemas 'support evolution' generically, without checking that the new field carries an explicit default. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Trap summary is symmetric: 'Adding OR REMOVING an Avro field without a default value breaks schema evolution outright.' The Avro specification says a writer field absent from the reader schema 'is ignored' -- removal never signals an error. Only the reader-has-a-field-with-no-default-that-the-writer-lacks direction gives 'an error is signalled.' A trap row that states its own rule imprecisely is worse than no trap; make the claim directional.]

subject: BACKWARD compatibility direction
description: BACKWARD compatibility means a schema registered as BACKWARD-compatible allows consumers using the NEW schema to read data produced with the LAST (older) schema. The common mistake is assuming BACKWARD means 'old consumers can still read new data' (that is actually FORWARD compatibility). Because of this, the safe rollout order under BACKWARD compatibility is: upgrade all consumers first, then let producers start writing the new schema. Teams that roll out in the opposite order (producers first) under a BACKWARD-only contract can have old consumers choke on data they cannot deserialize, or new consumers running ahead of a producer upgrade misinterpret events. Confluent's own docs are explicit that FORWARD compatibility, by contrast, requires producers to upgrade first.

subject: Protobuf field number reuse
description: Protobuf's own best-practices documentation states this without qualification: 'Never re-use a tag number. It messes up deserialization... Even if you think no one is using the field, don't re-use a tag number.' The mechanism: protobuf's wire format encodes only the field number and wire type, not the field name, so a message encoded under one schema and decoded under another that reassigned that number will silently misinterpret the bytes rather than erroring. The corrective governance practice, confirmed both in protobuf.dev and in Buf's breaking-change tool documentation (opened directly), is to mark deleted field numbers as `reserved` so the compiler itself blocks accidental reuse. Buf's `FIELD_NO_DELETE_UNLESS_NUMBER_RESERVED` rule mechanically enforces this at CI time rather than relying on developer memory.

subject: Buf breaking change detection quickstart
description: Confirmed by opening the page directly. Three progressive, concrete exercises against a real example repo (buf.build/tutorials/breaking): (1) local git comparison — add a new enum value and run detection against uncommitted changes; (2) BSR module comparison — rename an enum value (`PET_TYPE_HAMSTER` to `PET_TYPE_RODENT`), which buf correctly flags as breaking with the exact message shown on the page; (3) remote git comparison — move an enum into a new file and discover this breaks under the default FILE ruleset but not under the looser PACKAGE ruleset, directly demonstrating the strictness-ladder concept (FILE/PACKAGE/WIRE_JSON/WIRE) rather than just asserting it. Squarely in scope for schema-evolution/breaking-change governance practice.

subject: Confluent Schema Registry 101 — Evolve Existing Schemas hands-on
description: Confirmed by opening the page directly. Learner does two parallel tracks. Protobuf (UI): open the proto-purchase schema in Confluent Cloud Console, click 'Evolve Schema', add a new field (`string employee_id = 4;`), click 'Validate' to run the live compatibility check, save, and confirm the version incremented. Avro (local/CLI): edit purchase.avsc to add a field, run `./gradlew testSchemasTask` — which fails without a default value — then add `"default": "unknown"` and rerun until it succeeds, then run `./gradlew registerSchemasTask` to actually register the change. This is a genuinely hands-on exercise that makes the reader hit the exact failure this run's trap rows describe (Avro field with no default fails validation) and then fix it, rather than just reading about it. Part of the free Schema Registry 101 course on developer.confluent.io.

subject: Pact JS contract testing workshop
description: Confirmed by opening both the docs.pact.io landing page and the linked GitHub repo directly. Real, actively maintained repository (159 stars, 171 forks, 239 commits, open PRs/issues as of this check) under the official pact-foundation GitHub org. The README states the workshop takes 1-2 hours depending on depth. It progresses through 13 git-branch-tagged steps: writing a consumer test against a mock provider, generating a Pact contract, verifying it against a real Express provider, handling provider states, adding authorization, and finally publishing/consuming contracts via a Pact Broker (steps 11-12 need a locally-Dockerized broker or a PactFlow account). This is squarely in scope: consumer-driven contract testing hands-on practice.

subject: Pact JVM/Spring contract testing workshop
description: Confirmed by opening the GitHub repo directly: pact-foundation/pact-workshop-jvm-spring, 118 stars, 81 forks, 57 commits, Docker Compose support, current Spring Boot patterns, no signs of abandonment. The README states the workshop takes about 2 hours. It covers 11 progressive steps: consumer/provider setup, contract generation and verification (steps 1-5), missing-product and state-management scenarios (steps 6-7), authorization and request filtering (steps 8-10), and Pact Broker integration for cross-team publishing (step 11), built around a realistic e-commerce product-catalog scenario. Useful as the Java-ecosystem counterpart to the JS workshop already listed, for readers working in that stack.

subject: Azure Breaking Change Review Board approval gate
description: This documents breaking-change governance as an organizational process, not just a technical rule: a human review board sits in the approval path specifically because the cost of an unreviewed breaking change surfaces late, at the customer's next deployment, not at merge time. Azure additionally requires an azure-deprecating response header communicating what is retiring, the retirement date, and a documentation URL - the same header-plus-link pattern as RFC 9745/8594, applied as a mandatory internal policy rather than an optional client courtesy. [AUDIT viable->wounded: 'pull requests failing the policy check cannot merge without that approval' is not in the cited Azure Guidelines.md -- the document contains no pull-request or merge-gating text. The review-board rule itself is quoted correctly ('DO NOT introduce any breaking changes into the service'; breaking changes 'allowable... if approved by the Azure Breaking Change Reviewers but only following ample communication to customers and a lengthy deprecation period'). Drop the unsupported merge-gate clause.]

subject: Buf's four breaking-change strictness categories: FILE, PACKAGE, WIRE, WIRE_JSON
description: Which category an organization enforces is a governance decision with different blast radii: FILE catches source-level breakage that would fail a compile in strict languages like C++ or Python, while WIRE only cares whether bytes on the wire still decode correctly, tolerating renames and file moves that would break generated code. Choosing a looser category than your actual consumers need is a decision whose cost surfaces later, when a change Buf approved as 'non-breaking' still breaks a consumer that depended on generated-code stability Buf wasn't checking for.

subject: Compatibility mode choice dictates rollout order
description: Confluent's schema evolution documentation (opened directly) ties each compatibility mode to a specific safe deployment order: BACKWARD requires all consumers to upgrade before producers start writing the new schema; FORWARD requires all producers to upgrade first, and old data must be fully drained/unavailable before consumers upgrade; FULL allows producers and consumers to upgrade independently in any order, at the cost of requiring every change to satisfy both directions simultaneously (e.g., new fields must carry defaults so both old and new schemas can decode each other's data). TRANSITIVE variants extend the same guarantee across every historical schema version, not just the immediately previous one — meaningfully different in a topic with many schema versions in flight, since non-transitive BACKWARD only checks against the last version and can silently accumulate incompatibilities two or three versions back. Picking a mode is therefore a decision about which team (producer or consumer owners) is forced to move first during every future change, and that constraint is easy to discover only once a rollout goes wrong.

subject: Consumer-driven contract ownership
description: Martin Fowler's original Consumer-Driven Contracts article (opened directly) describes the pattern as consumer contracts expressing consumer expectations, adopted by the provider so that 'consumer contracts effectively define which parts of that provider contract currently support the business value realized by the system.' This is a judgment-level design decision, not a mechanical testing choice: it determines who has authority over what counts as a breaking change. A provider-authored contract can change anything the provider didn't anticipate a consumer needing; a consumer-driven contract makes any change that breaks a registered consumer expectation visible before release, at the cost of providers now depending on consumers actually maintaining and publishing their contracts (typically via a broker).

subject: Date-based API versioning as a governance model
description: Stripe's own engineering blog (opened directly) explains why they rejected major-version-number versioning: 'changes between versions being so big and so impactful for users that it's almost as painful as re-integrating from scratch,' and that scheme also forces a binary choice of freezing consumers on an old major version or cutting them off. Instead, Stripe pins every account to the API version active when it was created (a date, e.g. 2024-04-10); every incoming request for an older-pinned account is passed through a chain of small, per-change version-shim modules so that the internal service logic only ever has to implement the current schema, not a matrix of if/else branches for every historical version. This is a genuine judgment-level tradeoff: it adds real internal maintenance cost (an ever-growing chain of shims) in exchange for never forcing a disruptive re-integration on consumers, and is presented as a deliberate alternative to both URI-path and header-based major versioning.

subject: Deprecation and sunset process requirements
description: Zalando's public REST API guidelines (opened directly) lay out the concrete governance steps beyond headers: (1) the deprecation must be part of the API specification itself, with `deprecated: true` and a migration description, so it's discoverable by tooling, not just by inspecting live traffic; (2) for a sunset (full shutdown) to be permitted, the API owner must obtain explicit consumer/partner consent to a specific sunset date, negotiated as part of granting access in the first place for external partners; (3) the provider must monitor production usage of the deprecated surface to know whether consumers have actually migrated, and clients are expected to monitor the Deprecation/Sunset headers themselves and alert on them. This is a judgment call, not a mechanical step, because the 'reasonable time span' for the deprecation window has to be negotiated per-consumer and isn't dictated by the spec.

subject: Google AIP stability-level strategies: channel-, release-, and visibility-based
description: Choosing among these is a judgment call with different long-term costs: channel-based is Google's recommended default because it avoids proliferating short-lived version identifiers, release-based gives more predictability to specific cohorts of early consumers at the cost of more surfaces to maintain, and visibility-based avoids new version identifiers entirely but requires access-control infrastructure. The wrong choice doesn't fail on day one - it shows up as either channel churn, or too many concurrently-supported pre-release surfaces, months into the API's life.

subject: Google AIP: recommended 180-day deprecation window for beta releases
description: This is a concrete instance of the deprecation-window-length decision: too short and consumers who haven't migrated get broken; too long and the provider carries maintenance cost for versions it wants to retire. AIP-185 ties the number to release maturity (beta gets a shorter guaranteed window than GA), which is itself a judgment about how much stability a given maturity label should promise.

subject: JSON Schema's open vs. closed content model and its effect on compatibility
description: This is a schema-design judgment call specific to JSON Schema among the three serialization formats: an open model is more forgiving of producer-side additions (new fields simply pass through undeclared) but weaker at catching typos or unintended extra data; a closed model is stricter and catches those, but a producer that adds any new field without updating the reader schema will have every message rejected outright. The consequence of the wrong choice doesn't appear until the first field addition under a closed model, or the first unwanted-data leak under an open one - both late-surfacing costs typical of judgment-level knowledge.

subject: Microsoft Graph deprecation window: 24-36 months notice
description: This is a concrete, named organizational answer to 'how long should a deprecation window be' - a judgment-level decision the AIP-185 180-day beta figure sits in contrast to. The gap (180 days for a Google beta vs. 24-36 months for Microsoft Graph GA) reflects that maturity label (beta vs. GA) is itself the variable governing how long a provider is willing to commit to. Choosing a window that's too short for the surface's maturity is a decision whose cost only appears when consumers who relied on the longer implicit guarantee get broken. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Inverts the two windows. Microsoft Graph's guidelines state: 'you MUST create new element versions and support deprecated elements for a minimum of 36 MONTHS OR 24 MONTHS WITH DEMONSTRATED NON-USAGE.' 36 months is the baseline; 24 is the REDUCED window available only on demonstrated non-usage. The row leads with 24 months as the general commitment, so a reader takes away the wrong number.]

subject: No-versioning / continuous compatible-evolution strategy (Stripe's rolling dates)
description: Per Stripe's own versioning writeup, a new account is automatically pinned to the latest version on its first API call; it keeps working on that version indefinitely unless the developer explicitly upgrades (via the dashboard) or overrides per-request with a Stripe-Version header. Each dated version bundles a small set of changes rather than a large breaking rewrite, so upgrades are incremental rather than all-or-nothing. Choosing this strategy versus versioned major releases is a governance decision: it demands building and maintaining a per-version compatibility-transform layer (see the companion mechanism row on Stripe's transformer architecture) in exchange for consumers never facing a hard cutover deadline.

subject: NONE compatibility mode disables schema safety checks
description: This is a judgment-level trap-adjacent concept: choosing NONE removes the registry's only automated safety net, and the consequence (a deserialization failure in production) surfaces later, at read time on whichever consumer first encounters the incompatible data, not at schema-registration time. It's sometimes a legitimate choice (e.g. during early prototyping, or for topics with a single tightly-coupled producer/consumer pair deployed atomically) but the decision to use it needs to be deliberate, not a default left unconfigured.

subject: Protobuf's tiered classification of changes: wire-safe, wire-unsafe, and conditionally-safe
description: This three-way classification is itself a judgment tool: the middle band ('wire-compatible' but requiring careful rollout) is where teams get burned, because the change type-checks and appears safe in isolation, but produces different results depending on which side (producer or consumer) upgrades first - the cost of getting the rollout order wrong surfaces at scale, not in a single local test. Choosing to make one of these conditionally-safe changes without a deliberate rollout plan is exactly the kind of correct-syntax-wrong-decision failure that defines judgment-level knowledge. [AUDIT depth judgment->operation: Protobuf's wire-safe / wire-unsafe / conditionally-safe classification is the lookup table you need to make a schema change correctly in the normal case; without it the change breaks immediately and visibly at decode. Its siblings A-020, A-021 and A-026 are all operation. (Arguable: the conditionally-safe band carries rollout-ordering judgment; better to split that out than to tier the whole row up.)]

subject: Transitive compatibility checking (BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE / FORWARD_TRANSITIVE / FULL_TRANSITIVE) vs. latest-only
description: Choosing transitive vs. non-transitive is a judgment call whose cost is invisible until a consumer that's several versions behind - not just one version behind - tries to read current data, or a producer several versions behind writes into a topic a fresh consumer must read. Non-transitive checking is cheaper and looser day-to-day but silently permits a chain of individually-compatible changes that are not jointly compatible across the full history; transitive checking catches that at registration time but is stricter and can block legitimate-looking single-step changes. Confluent's docs present this explicitly as a config choice (global default or per-subject).

subject: Zalando deprecation process: deprecated:true plus consumer consent before sunset
description: This is a governance-process rule, not just a syntax rule: the mechanical marking (deprecated: true) is easy to get right, but the consent-gathering step is a judgment-laden negotiation whose cost surfaces late - at cutover, if any consumer never gave consent or never migrated, the shutdown either breaks that consumer or has to slip. Zalando additionally requires the Deprecation and Sunset headers to reflect the earliest timestamp when multiple elements are deprecated at once, and requires clients to build monitoring/alerting on those headers rather than relying on best-effort awareness.

subject: Zalando's rejection of URL versioning as a governance decision
description: This is a judgment-level example precisely because it contradicts the majority convention (used by Stripe, GitHub, and most public APIs per URI-path). Zalando's compatibility.adoc argues that a version number in the path forces every consumer to coordinate a URL change with every provider release, and that this coupling is worse than the added complexity of content-negotiation-based media types. The consequence of choosing wrongly is not visible immediately - both schemes 'work' on day one - it shows up later as either painful multi-version URL sprawl (URI scheme at scale) or brittle content-negotiation tooling and debugging friction (media-type scheme at scale).

subject: Adding a response field is always safe
description: A first-hand account (a team's own postmortem-style writeup) describes pushing what they believed was a purely additive JSON response change; three mobile apps crashed because they used strict JSON parsers that rejected the unexpected new field. The general pattern behind this trap: 'additive' is a schema-level judgment, but real consumers include code paths (strict deserializers, typed clients, PUT-based updates that round-trip and re-send a payload, systems with fixed-width storage columns) that are broken by fields they didn't ask for. The corrective framing from the same body of writing: treat additions as low-risk, not risk-free, and gate them behind the same contract-testing/consumer-visibility discipline as other changes rather than skipping review because 'it's just additive.'

subject: Contract tests as a substitute for integration tests
description: Microsoft's public Engineering Fundamentals Playbook, in its consumer-driven contract (CDC) testing chapter (opened directly), states: 'Contract tests are not the place to verify internal business logic and correctness of the consumer,' and cautions that CDC scope must be kept tight so it doesn't blur into 'other higher level functional testing layers.' The practical failure mode this guards against: a team adopts Pact-style contract tests, sees them pass, and treats that as equivalent coverage to a full integration or end-to-end suite — but contract tests only verify that a specific consumer-provider interaction matches an agreed shape; they say nothing about network behavior, infra, multi-service call sequencing, or a consumer's own business logic. Related literature (Martin Fowler's original Consumer-Driven Contracts article, opened directly) frames CDC instead as a design discipline: consumers author the contract to make the provider's evolution safe for them, which is a narrower and different goal than end-to-end verification.

subject: Deprecation header as a complete deprecation process
description: RFC 8594 (the Sunset HTTP header) is explicit about its own limits: it defines the header as a way to 'signal intent so that applications using resources may get a warning ahead of time,' and states plainly that 'what an appropriate reaction is... is outside the scope of this specification.' The RFC also says the Sunset header is not even appropriate for the early stage where an API is deprecated-but-still-working — only for the final unresponsive stage — meaning header-only signaling misses the whole early phase of a real deprecation. Zalando's public API guidelines, opened directly, mandate a much larger process around the header: the deprecation must be reflected in the machine-readable API spec (`deprecated: true` with a migration description), the provider must get explicit consumer consent to a sunset date before shutting anything down, and the provider must monitor actual usage of the deprecated surface in production to know when it's safe to sunset — none of which a response header alone provides.

subject: Protobuf required fields
description: Protobuf's official best-practices guide advises: 'Never add a required field, instead add // required to document the API contract' (i.e., convey the requirement in a comment/convention, not the wire schema). The rationale given is about the direction time moves in schema evolution: a field that seems logically required today may need to become optional or removed years later, and once a field is wire-level required, no future version can safely drop that requirement without breaking every client still enforcing it — an intentionally stricter feature becomes a one-way door. Teams that reach for `required` because it look like better data-quality enforcement are trading a short-term validation win for a long-term evolution hazard.

subject: URI-path versioning has no cost
description: Troy Hunt's long-running, widely-referenced piece on API versioning argues against the idea that any one versioning mechanism is simple or costless. He makes the semantic case against URI versioning directly: 'URLs suck [as a versioning mechanism] because they should represent the entity' — the resource is the same resource regardless of representation version, so baking version into the URI conflates identity with representation. He also concedes the practical case for it (shareable, clickable, cache-friendly URLs) but is explicit that the header/Accept-based alternative has its own real cost (you lose a pastable URL; clients must construct requests carefully). His conclusion is not 'URI versioning is right' or 'wrong' but that teams treating their chosen scheme as free of tradeoffs, in either direction, are wrong — 'None of these are bad in any tangible sense... they're just different.' The trap is skipping the tradeoff analysis because URI versioning looks like the default, low-effort choice.

subject: Avro enum default symbol enables forward-evolution of enums
description: This behavior is mechanism-level: it doesn't affect the normal case where every consumer already knows every enum value, so nobody encounters it operationally under everyday conditions. It only manifests in the novel situation of a producer emitting a newly-added symbol that a not-yet-upgraded consumer has never seen - exactly the scenario where a reader who only knows 'add fields with defaults' would incorrectly assume enums evolve the same way, or would be surprised the read doesn't simply throw. [AUDIT depth mechanism->operation: The Avro enum 'default' symbol is a concrete schema feature a reader applies, in the same class as A-007 (aliases) and A-008 (field defaults), both correctly at operation. Failure signature is 'you add an enum value and consumers break immediately and visibly', which is operation, not 'you cannot predict behavior you have not already seen'. Reads as assigned by how advanced 'schema resolution' sounds rather than against the failure-signature table.]

subject: Stripe's version-transformer chain architecture
description: This is mechanism-level knowledge: it doesn't change how any single API call behaves in the normal case (a developer calling a pinned version just gets that version's shape, which is operation-level to use), but it explains behavior you can't predict without having seen the internals - for instance, why a single conceptual field change might appear at a different position or format depending on how many version-transform steps a given dated version sits behind current, or why Stripe's core business logic stays free of accumulated if/else version checks despite supporting essentially every version issued since 2011.

subject: Derive rollout order from a compatibility mode, and back again
description: Start from the mode and derive the order. Then reverse: given a deployment where you cannot upgrade all consumers first, derive which mode you are forced into. Reversing is the half that catches a memorized mapping, because the direction of BACKWARD is the single most commonly inverted fact in this area.

subject: Draft a deprecation timeline with every required signal
description: Produce the actual timeline with dates. Include the Deprecation and Sunset headers with correct relative ordering, the link relation to the policy document, the notice window and your justification for its length, and how you determine whether every affected consumer has migrated. Then answer whether you may shut down without their consent, and what your answer depends on.

subject: Run the same schema change through Avro and Protobuf
description: Add a field, remove a field, rename a field, and change a field's type. For each, decide safety under Avro's resolution rules and under Protobuf's wire rules. The differences are not arbitrary: Avro resolves by name against a reader schema, Protobuf resolves by field number on the wire. Being able to state that sentence is the exit condition.

subject: State what a contract test catches that an integration test does not
description: Write a concrete breakage that a consumer-driven contract test catches and an integration test misses, and one the reverse. Then name a class of failure neither catches. The third answer is the one that shows you understand what contract testing actually buys.

subject: Triage a change list into breaking, non-breaking, and depends-on-consumer
description: Write ten changes: add optional response field, add required request field, remove an enum value, widen an int to a long, rename a field, tighten validation, change a default, reorder an array, add an error code, change a timeout. Sort into breaking, non-breaking, and depends. The third pile is the real exercise, and the consumer assumption that decides it is the thing worth being able to say out loud.

subject: Schema Registry's default compatibility mode is BACKWARD
description: Confluent's schema-evolution documentation states that 'the default compatibility mode is BACKWARD', checked non-transitively against the latest registered version only. This matters more than a default usually does, because BACKWARD is not a neutral setting: per the same page it permits adding optional fields and removing fields, and it fixes the rollout order -- consumers upgrade before producers. A team that never touches the compatibility configuration has therefore made a governance decision (A-033) without knowing it, and will find out at the first rollout where a producer ships first. It also explains a common surprise: a schema change rejected by a registry nobody configured is being rejected by BACKWARD's rules specifically, not by generic 'schema validation'. Added by audit: six rows in this set discuss selecting among the modes (A-001, A-022, A-025, A-033, A-043, A-045) and none states which one applies by default.

subject: The tolerant reader: consumers must accept compatible extensions
description: Zalando's compatibility chapter carries the rule '{MUST} prepare clients to accept compatible API extensions', instructing that 'service clients should apply the robustness principle' and specifically 'be tolerant with unknown fields in the payload', citing Fowler's TolerantReader and the ACM piece 'The Robustness Principle Reconsidered'. This is the hinge the rest of the topic hangs on. Every claim in this row set that an additive change is non-breaking -- Microsoft Graph's 'adding new elements is allowed and is not considered a breaking change' (A-016), Protobuf's 'adding new fields is safe' (A-044), Avro's writer-field-ignored rule (A-008), Schema Registry's BACKWARD mode permitting added fields (A-022) -- is conditional on the consumer being a tolerant reader. It is also the direct explanation of the A-048 trap: adding a response field is safe against a tolerant reader and breaks a strict-parsing or round-tripping client, which is exactly why Microsoft's guidelines require each service to publish its own definition of breaking (A-002). Choosing a strict parser is a decision whose cost lands late, on someone else's compatible deploy. Added by audit: the run opened this file twice (A-004, A-047) and took the versioning sections roughly ninety lines below this rule without taking the rule, leaving the topic's entire consumer-side obligation unrepresented across 59 API rows.
